stem:
A woman at 27+5 weeks is in established preterm labour, 6 cm dilated, and birth is expected within about two hours. She received her first dose of betamethasone an hour ago. Her blood pressure is normal and she has no features of pre-eclampsia. The registrar asks whether intravenous magnesium sulfate is still worth starting.

What should the obstetrician advise?

options.label: A
options.text: Withhold it, as she has no features of pre-eclampsia
options.explanation: Magnesium for fetal neuroprotection does not depend on pre-eclampsia; the indication here is imminent birth before 30 weeks.

options.label: B
options.text: Withhold it, as two hours is too short for any benefit
options.explanation: Benefit is greatest with a few hours of infusion before birth, but it should still be started when birth is expected sooner. Birth is not delayed to complete it.

options.label: C
options.text: Start it, mainly to delay birth for the steroids
options.explanation: Magnesium is not being used as a tocolytic here and does not reliably delay birth.

options.label: D
options.text: Start it, mainly to boost surfactant after steroids
options.explanation: Faster surfactant production is the corticosteroid’s effect; magnesium does not add to lung maturation.

options.label: E
options.text: Start it now, to lower the baby’s risk of cerebral palsy
options.explanation: Magnesium sulfate before birth at under 30 weeks reduces the risk of cerebral palsy in the child. Start it now, even though birth may come before the infusion is complete.

context: Give magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection when birth before 30 weeks is imminent, even without pre-eclampsia and even if little time remains.
